easy.explanation: Isaiah 45:1 says, “Thus saith the Lord to his anointed, to Cyrus.”
easy.q: To whom does the Lord address the words “to his anointed”?

easy.explanation: The Lord promises “to open before him the two leaved gates.”
easy.q: What does the Lord promise to open before Cyrus?

answers: Treasures of darkness and hidden riches
easy.explanation: Isaiah 45:3 speaks of “the treasures of darkness, and hidden riches of secret places.”
easy.q: What does the Lord promise to give Cyrus?

answers: So Cyrus may build a palace
So Cyrus may know that the Lord has called him by name
So Cyrus may rule over Israel
medium.explanation: The treasures are given so that Cyrus may know who has called him.
medium.q: Why does the Lord give Cyrus hidden treasures?

medium.explanation: The Lord says, “For Jacob my servant’s sake, and Israel mine elect.”
medium.q: For whose sake does the Lord call Cyrus?

answers: I hid you from your enemies
medium.explanation: To gird Cyrus means to strengthen or equip him for his appointed work.
medium.q: What does “I girded thee” mean in this passage?

answers: God can work through a ruler who does not yet know Him
Israel had no place in God’s plan
challenge.explanation: The passage twice notes that Cyrus did not know the Lord, yet God directed him.
challenge.q: What important truth is shown by the Lord strengthening Cyrus even though Cyrus did not know Him?

answers: That Cyrus alone ruled the world
That there is no God besides the Lord
challenge.explanation: The Lord says that people may know “that there is none beside me.”
challenge.q: What were people to recognize through the Lord’s actions?

answers: It connects God’s work with righteousness and salvation
It removes Cyrus from the passage
It describes only a military battle
challenge.explanation: The verse pictures righteousness falling from heaven and salvation springing from the earth.
challenge.q: How does verse 8 expand the description of God’s work?

answers: A potsherd or piece of clay
easy.explanation: The passage compares such a person to a potsherd and clay before the one who fashions it.
easy.q: What is a person compared to when he strives with his Maker?

easy.explanation: The Lord says, “I have made the earth” and “my hands have stretched out the heavens.”
easy.q: Who made the earth and stretched out the heavens?

answers: Build God’s city and release the captives
easy.explanation: The Lord says of Cyrus, “he shall build my city, and he shall let go my captives.”
easy.q: What would Cyrus do according to verse 13?

answers: People are limited and cannot dictate God’s actions
Clay is stronger than its maker
medium.explanation: The image shows that the created thing cannot question or command its maker.
medium.q: What does the comparison between clay and its maker teach?

answers: Both are under the Lord’s authority
medium.explanation: The Creator of heaven and earth is also the one who raised up Cyrus.
medium.q: What connection does the passage make between creation and Cyrus’s mission?

answers: A challenge to the Maker’s actions
medium.explanation: The question portrays the created thing improperly challenging the one who fashioned it.
medium.q: What does the phrase “What makest thou?” express?

answers: They show the creature judging its Creator
challenge.explanation: The clay has no rightful basis for judging or correcting the potter.
challenge.q: Why are questions such as “What makest thou?” presented as improper?

answers: The release required a great payment
The release was given without payment or bribe
challenge.explanation: The Lord states that Cyrus would release the captives without receiving a price or reward.
challenge.q: What does “not for price nor reward” mean concerning the release of the captives?

answers: The Lord created the earth, humanity, and the heavens
The Lord does not act in the world
challenge.explanation: The Creator has authority over everything He has made.
challenge.q: Why should people not dictate God’s actions?

paragraphs.title: The Hidden God and Israel’s Salvation

answers: The people of Egypt, Ethiopia, and the Sabeans
easy.explanation: Verse 14 names Egypt, Ethiopia, and the Sabeans as those who would come in submission.
easy.q: Who would come to Israel and bow down before it?

answers: They would be ashamed and confounded
easy.explanation: The verse says that the makers of idols would be “ashamed” and “confounded.”
easy.q: What would happen to the makers of idols?

easy.explanation: Israel shall be saved “with an everlasting salvation.”
easy.q: What kind of salvation is promised to Israel?

answers: They recognize that God is in Israel and that there is no other God
They want to hide their idols
medium.explanation: They confess, “Surely God is in thee; and there is none else, there is no God.”
medium.q: Why do the nations come to Israel according to the passage?

answers: The earth was made without purpose
God made the earth for habitation and order
medium.explanation: God did not create the earth in vain; He formed it to be inhabited.
medium.q: What does the statement that the earth was formed “to be inhabited” teach?

answers: A god who does not exist
A God whose work is not always openly visible
A god found only in one temple
medium.explanation: The phrase recognizes that God may work mysteriously while still being Israel’s Saviour.
medium.q: What does “a God that hidest thyself” mean in this context?

answers: The idol makers are ashamed, while Israel is saved and not ashamed
Both are saved in the same way
Israel makes idols, while the idol makers are saved
challenge.explanation: The passage contrasts the shame of idol makers with Israel’s everlasting salvation.
challenge.q: What contrast is made between the makers of idols and Israel?

answers: The Lord speaks righteousness and declares what is right
The Lord refuses to speak to Jacob
The Lord speaks only through idols
challenge.explanation: The Lord says, “I speak righteousness, I declare things that are right.”
challenge.q: What does “I have not spoken in secret” reveal about the Lord’s message?

answers: Idol makers are ashamed, while the Lord saves Israel
challenge.explanation: The passage presents idols as powerless and the Lord as the true Saviour.
challenge.q: How do these verses show the Lord’s superiority over idols?

paragraphs.title: A Call to All Nations for Salvation

answers: All the ends of the earth
easy.explanation: The Lord addresses “all the ends of the earth.”
easy.q: To whom is the invitation “Look unto me, and be ye saved” given?

easy.explanation: The people worship a god “that cannot save.”
easy.q: What can the idols not do?

easy.explanation: The final verse says, “In the Lord shall all the seed of Israel be justified, and shall glory.”
easy.q: What will all the seed of Israel do in the Lord?

answers: They should look to Him and be saved
They should make a larger image
medium.explanation: The Lord calls the nations to look to Him for salvation.
medium.q: What does the Lord offer the nations instead of trusting idols?

answers: Every knee will bow and every tongue will swear
The idols will rule the world
medium.explanation: The Lord declares that every knee shall bow and every tongue shall swear.
medium.q: What will ultimately happen to every knee and every tongue?

medium.explanation: The phrase refers to those who have escaped or survived among the nations.
medium.q: What are “they that are escaped of the nations”?

answers: The Lord is the only God
challenge.explanation: The repetition emphasizes the Lord’s unique and unmatched deity.
challenge.q: What does the repeated statement “there is none else” emphasize?

answers: The oath guarantees that all creation will acknowledge His authority
The oath removes Israel from the promise
The oath concerns only idol makers
challenge.explanation: Every knee bowing and every tongue swearing expresses universal acknowledgment of the Lord.
challenge.q: What is the connection between the Lord’s oath and worldwide recognition of Him?

answers: Israel is justified and glories in the Lord
Israel remains separated from all nations
challenge.explanation: The chapter closes by saying that all the seed of Israel shall be justified and shall glory in the Lord.
challenge.q: How is Israel’s position described at the end of the chapter?
